title: AI Cystoscopy
abstract: Systematic review type: PRISMA-DTA systematic review with conditional bivariate meta-analysis (Reitsma model), with three co-primary units of analysis (patient / lesion / image) synthesised sepa-rately. Registration: OSF Registries. POPULATION Adults (≥18 years) undergoing white-light cystoscopy (flexible office cystoscopy, rigid cystoscopy or transurethral resection) for suspected bladder cancer (haematuria, suspicious imaging, positive cytology) or for surveillance after conservative treatment of non-muscle-invasive bladder can-cer (NMIBC). Clinical context (primary detection vs surveillance) is a pre-specified subgroup variable; “not reported” is coded as such. Eligible data: prospectively or retrospectively collected cystoscopic still images or videos from human patients, including publicly released datasets, provided the origin of the images is traceable to a clinical cohort. Exclusions: paediatric populations; upper urinary tract endosco-py (ureteroscopy); phantom, animal or fully synthetic image sets; cohorts in which the target condition is not a bladder tumour. INDEX TEST Any artificial-intelligence system trained on cystoscopic image or video data (classical ma-chine learning, convolutional, transformer or hybrid deep learning; classification, object detection, se-mantic/instance segmentation) applied to cystoscopic images or videos acquired under white light, to identify bladder tumours, and evaluated on data independent of model training. The defining criterion is the acquisition modality: white-light cystoscopy without optical filtering or exogenous contrast agent. Purely software-based transformations of white-light frames applied downstream of acquisition (e.g., simulated spectral or hyperspectral conversion) are considered part of the AI pipeline and are eligible, coded as a covariate; when a standard white-light arm is reported alongside, both are extracted. The model output must be binarisable (tumour vs non-tumour) at a stated decision rule so that a 2×2 table is extractable or algebraically reconstructible; segmentation or detection studies reporting only overlap or detection metrics (Dice, IoU, mAP) without a 2×2 table are retained for narrative synthesis only. Studies combining white-light with enhanced imaging (NBI, blue light/PDD) are eligible only if a white-light-specific 2×2 table can be extracted; otherwise excluded (no white-light-specific data). Exclusions: gen-eral-purpose multimodal large language models used without task-specific training on cystoscopy data; blue-light/photodynamic diagnosis or NBI as the sole acquisition modality; confocal laser endomicros-copy and optical coherence tomography; Raman and other spectroscopies; CT/MR virtual cystoscopy; AI for surgical-phase recognition, image enhancement, stitching or 3D reconstruction without diagnostic accuracy outcomes. REFERENCE STANDARD Positive cases: histopathology from biopsy or transurethral resection. Negative cases: histopathology, clinical follow-up, or cystoscopy judged normal by the urologist; the method of verification is recorded for each study. Studies whose negative cases rest on the urologist’s judgement alone are eligible and included in the main pool, and rated High risk of bias in the QUADAS-2 reference-standard domain; a pre-specified sen-sitivity analysis is restricted to studies with histologically or follow-up–verified negative cases (≥6 months). Datasets in which positive labels derive from expert visual annotation without histological confirmation are retained for narrative synthesis only. Exclusions: no reference standard; reference limited to another AI output. DIAGNOSIS OF INTEREST Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder, any stage (Ta, T1, ≥T2), including carcinoma in situ, versus non-tumoural findings (normal mucosa, inflammation/cystitis, post-resection scar, other benign lesions). Non-urothelial bladder malignancies are included when reported within a mixed tumour class and cod-ed. Secondary target: tumour grade (low vs high) as a separate estimand, meta-analysed if at least 4 studies provide a 2×2 table, otherwise synthesised narratively; stage/invasion prediction from white-light im-ages: narrative only. STUDY DESIGN Eligible: diagnostic accuracy studies (prospective or retrospective; cohort or case-control/“two-gate” designs, the latter with an anticipated QUADAS-2 High rating on patient selection); reader studies com-paring AI with urologists on the same test set; randomised trials comparing AI-supported with standard white-light endoscopy, whose between-arm accuracy data are handled under the comparative question; full-length peer-reviewed conference proceedings papers with methods and results. Exclusions: conference abstracts and conference reviews; reviews, editorials, letters, protocols and trial-registry entries without results; dataset descriptors without a diagnostic evaluation; case reports; non-human studies. OUTCOMES Primary: sensitivity and specificity with a reconstructible 2×2 table (TP, FP, FN, TN), extracted separate-ly for each unit of analysis (patient, lesion, image/frame); units are never pooled together. Secondary: AUC, PPV/NPV, DOR, likelihood ratios; AI vs urologist accuracy on the same test set; urolo-gist-with-AI vs urologist-alone; tumour-grade accuracy; clinical-impact outcomes from randomised trials (detection rate, missed lesions, procedure time) described narratively. For studies without a reconstructible 2×2 table, the corresponding author is contacted (initial e‑mail at day 0, reminder at day 5, cutoff at day 10; all attempts documented); if the data are not obtained, the study is included in the narrative synthesis only. PRE-SPECIFIED ANALYSES Bivariate random-effects (Reitsma) meta-analysis conducted separately for each of the three co-primary units of analysis (patient, lesion, image); all clinical contexts are combined in the principal pool of each unit, and clinical context (primary detection / surveillance / not reported) is analysed as a pre-specified subgroup variable (see below). Feasibility: at least 4 studies per pool → bivariate model; fewer than 4 → narrative synthesis. No unit is designated as the single primary result; the three pools are reported with equal status. One data point per study and per unit, selected by a pre-defined rule (authors’ pre-specified threshold or designated primary model, then the most rigorous validation regime providing a 2×2 table: external > hold-out > nested cross-validation > k-fold), never the best-performing configura-tion. One entry per independent test cohort in the quantitative pool: when several reports share the same patients, the report is selected by a pre-defined, performance-blind rule (original publication for public benchmark datasets; otherwise: exploitable 2×2 table and reference standard > most rigorous validation regime > most complete cohort description > largest test set in patients > most recent); the other reports are described narratively. The same trained system evaluated on distinct test cohorts con-tributes one data point per cohort. Comparative analysis AI vs urologist (same test set): bivariate model with test-type covariate if at least 4 paired studies (a within-study paired comparison, hence a lower threshold than for between-study covariates); narrative otherwise; QUADAS-C applied. Pre-specified subgroup variables: clinical context, acquisition setting (office flexible cystoscopy vs oper-ating-room rigid/TURBT), input type (still images vs video/real-time), validation regime (internal vs external), task type (classification / detection / segmentation), software-transformed vs standard white-light frames, lesion morphology (flat/CIS vs papillary), model architecture family (classical machine learning / convolutional / transformer or hybrid), and two-gate vs single-gate design. For each variable, every level containing at least 4 studies is pooled separately with the bivariate model and its summary sensitivity and specificity (with 95% confidence and prediction regions) reported; levels with fewer than 4 studies are described narratively. A formal test of the difference between levels is performed only when the variable is informative in at least 10 studies within the pool, by entering it as a covariate in the bivariate model; the same ≥10-study threshold governs univariable meta-regression on continuous study-level covariates (publication year, training-set size, prevalence). All subgroup and meta-regression analyses are declared exploratory. Sensitivity analyses: restriction to studies with verified negative cases (histology or follow-up ≥6 months); exclusion of QUADAS-2 overall High; exclusion of PROBAST+AI Analysis High; exclusion of two-gate designs; external-validation results only; alternative validation regime when several 2×2 tables are reported; leave-one-out; alternative report per shared cohort. Heterogeneity: 95% prediction region as the primary indicator, τ² for logit sensitivity and specificity in support, I² reported only if required and never interpreted alone. Publication bias: Deeks’ funnel-plot asymmetry test computed separately for each pool (one per unit of analysis) with at least 10 studies; otherwise a reasoned statement. TEMPORAL AND LANGUAGE FRAME No lower date limit. Search cutoff: to be fixed at OSF deposit. Lan-guage: English only. Peer-reviewed publications only; preprints excluded. CERTAINTY OF EVIDENCE GRADE approach for diagnostic test accuracy applied to each primary esti-mand (sensitivity and specificity, per unit of analysis, and per clinical context where a context-specific pooled estimate is available), with a summary-of-findings table expressing true/false positives and neg-atives per 1000 patients at pre-specified prevalences of 15% and 20%. POPULATION Adults (≥18 years) undergoing white-light cystoscopy (flexible office cystoscopy, rigid cystoscopy or transurethral resection) for suspected bladder cancer (haematuria, suspicious imaging, positive cytology) or for surveillance after conservative treatment of non-muscle-invasive bladder can-cer (NMIBC). Clinical context (primary detection vs surveillance) is a pre-specified subgroup variable; “not reported” is coded as such. Eligible data: prospectively or retrospectively collected cystoscopic still images or videos from human patients, including publicly released datasets, provided the origin of the images is traceable to a clinical cohort. Exclusions: paediatric populations; upper urinary tract endosco-py (ureteroscopy); phantom, animal or fully synthetic image sets; cohorts in which the target condition is not a bladder tumour. INDEX TEST Any artificial-intelligence system trained on cystoscopic image or video data (classical ma-chine learning, convolutional, transformer or hybrid deep learning; classification, object detection, se-mantic/instance segmentation) applied to cystoscopic images or videos acquired under white light, to identify bladder tumours, and evaluated on data independent of model training. The defining criterion is the acquisition modality: white-light cystoscopy without optical filtering or exogenous contrast agent. Purely software-based transformations of white-light frames applied downstream of acquisition (e.g., simulated spectral or hyperspectral conversion) are considered part of the AI pipeline and are eligible, coded as a covariate; when a standard white-light arm is reported alongside, both are extracted. The model output must be binarisable (tumour vs non-tumour) at a stated decision rule so that a 2×2 table is extractable or algebraically reconstructible; segmentation or detection studies reporting only overlap or detection metrics (Dice, IoU, mAP) without a 2×2 table are retained for narrative synthesis only. Studies combining white-light with enhanced imaging (NBI, blue light/PDD) are eligible only if a white-light-specific 2×2 table can be extracted; otherwise excluded (no white-light-specific data). Exclusions: gen-eral-purpose multimodal large language models used without task-specific training on cystoscopy data; blue-light/photodynamic diagnosis or NBI as the sole acquisition modality; confocal laser endomicros-copy and optical coherence tomography; Raman and other spectroscopies; CT/MR virtual cystoscopy; AI for surgical-phase recognition, image enhancement, stitching or 3D reconstruction without diagnostic accuracy outcomes. REFERENCE STANDARD Positive cases: histopathology from biopsy or transurethral resection. Negative cases: histopathology, clinical follow-up, or cystoscopy judged normal by the urologist; the method of verification is recorded for each study. Studies whose negative cases rest on the urologist’s judgement alone are eligible and included in the main pool, and rated High risk of bias in the QUADAS-2 reference-standard domain; a pre-specified sen-sitivity analysis is restricted to studies with histologically or follow-up–verified negative cases (≥6 months). Datasets in which positive labels derive from expert visual annotation without histological confirmation are retained for narrative synthesis only. Exclusions: no reference standard; reference limited to another AI output. DIAGNOSIS OF INTEREST Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder, any stage (Ta, T1, ≥T2), including carcinoma in situ, versus non-tumoural findings (normal mucosa, inflammation/cystitis, post-resection scar, other benign lesions). Non-urothelial bladder malignancies are included when reported within a mixed tumour class and cod-ed. Secondary target: tumour grade (low vs high) as a separate estimand, meta-analysed if at least 4 studies provide a 2×2 table, otherwise synthesised narratively; stage/invasion prediction from white-light im-ages: narrative only. STUDY DESIGN Eligible: diagnostic accuracy studies (prospective or retrospective; cohort or case-control/“two-gate” designs, the latter with an anticipated QUADAS-2 High rating on patient selection); reader studies com-paring AI with urologists on the same test set; randomised trials comparing AI-supported with standard white-light endoscopy, whose between-arm accuracy data are handled under the comparative question; full-length peer-reviewed conference proceedings papers with methods and results. Exclusions: conference abstracts and conference reviews; reviews, editorials, letters, protocols and trial-registry entries without results; dataset descriptors without a diagnostic evaluation; case reports; non-human studies. OUTCOMES Primary: sensitivity and specificity with a reconstructible 2×2 table (TP, FP, FN, TN), extracted separate-ly for each unit of analysis (patient, lesion, image/frame); units are never pooled together. Secondary: AUC, PPV/NPV, DOR, likelihood ratios; AI vs urologist accuracy on the same test set; urolo-gist-with-AI vs urologist-alone; tumour-grade accuracy; clinical-impact outcomes from randomised trials (detection rate, missed lesions, procedure time) described narratively. For studies without a reconstructible 2×2 table, the corresponding author is contacted (initial e‑mail at day 0, reminder at day 5, cutoff at day 10; all attempts documented); if the data are not obtained, the study is included in the narrative synthesis only. PRE-SPECIFIED ANALYSES Bivariate random-effects (Reitsma) meta-analysis conducted separately for each of the three co-primary units of analysis (patient, lesion, image); all clinical contexts are combined in the principal pool of each unit, and clinical context (primary detection / surveillance / not reported) is analysed as a pre-specified subgroup variable (see below). Feasibility: at least 4 studies per pool → bivariate model; fewer than 4 → narrative synthesis. No unit is designated as the single primary result; the three pools are reported with equal status. One data point per study and per unit, selected by a pre-defined rule (authors’ pre-specified threshold or designated primary model, then the most rigorous validation regime providing a 2×2 table: external > hold-out > nested cross-validation > k-fold), never the best-performing configura-tion. One entry per independent test cohort in the quantitative pool: when several reports share the same patients, the report is selected by a pre-defined, performance-blind rule (original publication for public benchmark datasets; otherwise: exploitable 2×2 table and reference standard > most rigorous validation regime > most complete cohort description > largest test set in patients > most recent); the other reports are described narratively. The same trained system evaluated on distinct test cohorts con-tributes one data point per cohort. Comparative analysis AI vs urologist (same test set): bivariate model with test-type covariate if at least 4 paired studies (a within-study paired comparison, hence a lower threshold than for between-study covariates); narrative otherwise; QUADAS-C applied. Pre-specified subgroup variables: clinical context, acquisition setting (office flexible cystoscopy vs oper-ating-room rigid/TURBT), input type (still images vs video/real-time), validation regime (internal vs external), task type (classification / detection / segmentation), software-transformed vs standard white-light frames, lesion morphology (flat/CIS vs papillary), model architecture family (classical machine learning / convolutional / transformer or hybrid), and two-gate vs single-gate design. For each variable, every level containing at least 4 studies is pooled separately with the bivariate model and its summary sensitivity and specificity (with 95% confidence and prediction regions) reported; levels with fewer than 4 studies are described narratively. A formal test of the difference between levels is performed only when the variable is informative in at least 10 studies within the pool, by entering it as a covariate in the bivariate model; the same ≥10-study threshold governs univariable meta-regression on continuous study-level covariates (publication year, training-set size, prevalence). All subgroup and meta-regression analyses are declared exploratory. Sensitivity analyses: restriction to studies with verified negative cases (histology or follow-up ≥6 months); exclusion of QUADAS-2 overall High; exclusion of PROBAST+AI Analysis High; exclusion of two-gate designs; external-validation results only; alternative validation regime when several 2×2 tables are reported; leave-one-out; alternative report per shared cohort. Heterogeneity: 95% prediction region as the primary indicator, τ² for logit sensitivity and specificity in support, I² reported only if required and never interpreted alone. Publication bias: Deeks’ funnel-plot asymmetry test computed separately for each pool (one per unit of analysis) with at least 10 studies; otherwise a reasoned statement. TEMPORAL AND LANGUAGE FRAME No lower date limit. Search cutoff: to be fixed at OSF deposit. Lan-guage: English only. Peer-reviewed publications only; preprints excluded. CERTAINTY OF EVIDENCE GRADE approach for diagnostic test accuracy applied to each primary esti-mand (sensitivity and specificity, per unit of analysis, and per clinical context where a context-specific pooled estimate is available), with a summary-of-findings table expressing true/false positives and neg-atives per 1000 patients at pre-specified prevalences of 15% and 20%. title: DAR ‐ SAC : Dynamic Adaptive Regularization Soft Actor‐Critic
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes the dynamic adaptive regularization soft actor‐critic (DAR‐SAC) framework. The framework is based on the SAC algorithm, which is a reinforcement learning framework incorporating dynamic environment detection and adaptive optimization, to address the fixed exploration noise stiffness of the traditional SAC algorithm in dynamic environments. For the problems of fixed exploration noise rigidity, strategy oscillation aggravation and Q‐value over‐estimation in traditional SAC algorithms in dynamic environments, this paper firstly introduces a dynamic environment detection module to enable the robot to distinguish dynamic environments, and then combines the hybrid regularization mechanism and adaptive gradient trimming to accelerate convergence while suppressing abrupt changes in the strategy. In the constructed 3D point cloud simulation environment, the DAR‐SAC algorithm achieves significantly higher cumulative rewards and lower collision rates compared with SAC, SARC, DDPG, and TD3 algorithms. To further evaluate the robustness of the proposed framework against non‐stationary environments, we conduct extensive comparisons with state‐of‐the‐art variants, including SAC with adaptive entropy scheduling (SAC + AES), distributional SAC with three refinements (DSAC‐T), and SAC with delayed actor updates and replay mixing (SAC + DA + RM). The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits superior path‐planning performance in complex static and dynamic environments.

title: Continual learning via ensemble-based depth-wise masked autoencoders for data quality monitoring in high-energy physics
abstract: Abstract Machine learning (ML) techniques have been demonstrated to improve the accuracy and efficiency of anomaly detection (AD) when compared to conventional methods. This has led to the adoption of ML for data quality monitoring (DQM) use cases in order to monitor the operation of certain systems to ensure that they are free of undesirable or potentially deleterious anomalies. For applications in the field of High-Energy physics (HEP), where detectors must operate in long-running, harsh environments, ML models used in DQM that have been trained on static datasets are bound to experience degraded performance due to distributional shifts that naturally occur in the incoming data streams, unless directly mitigated via the inclusion of continual ML techniques. This work introduces DepthViT, a lightweight masked autoencoder architecture that employs unique depth-wise embeddings and depth-wise attention, to perform computationally efficient AD tasks. A continual learning framework is developed in which DepthViT models trained on the most recent data streams are ensembled with older models to create a robust overall system which is more resilient to shifts in incoming data streams. When evaluated on occupancy maps from the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) hadron calorimeter across multiple data-taking campaigns, the proposed method maintains precision above 98.8% and a stable ratio of correct anomaly predictions to number of anomalies both under small and large distributional shifts. Beyond HEP, the same ensembling-based continual adaptation strategy can be directly applied to industrial monitoring environments where data also naturally evolve over time. This work therefore presents a path toward adaptive anomaly detection systems capable of sustained operation in dynamic data environments.

title: Adaptive wavelet-CNN-LSTM forecasting with Bayesian optimization and SHAP interpretability for short-term solar irradiance prediction in a hot arid climate
abstract: Abstract Short-term global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting is essential for solar grid integration in hot arid sites due to atmospheric variability and dust aerosols. This study proposes a hybrid deep learning (DL) pipeline that combines Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers for 15-min GHI forecasting at a site in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Wavelet decomposition and model hyperparameters are jointly optimized using Optuna’s Bayesian search across 20 trials, and SHAP-based feature selection retains only the most informative predictors. Uncertainty is quantified through Monte Carlo dropout across 100 stochastic forward passes with a dropout rate of 0.2. The model is evaluated on 105,312 meteorological records using five-fold time-series cross-validation. Across all observations, the model achieves a mean RMSE of 6.62 ± 2.22 W/m 2 and an R 2 of 0.98 ± 0.01. Daytime-filtered evaluation (GHI > 50 W/m 2 ) yields a mean RMSE of 8.28 ± 1.45 W/m 2 and an R 2 of 0.961 ± 0.015, providing a more conservative estimate of forecasting accuracy during operationally relevant periods. The full pipeline reduces RMSE by 28–40% compared to ablated model variants and achieves a 47% reduction compared to the persistence baseline. The proposed pipeline delivers interpretable solar irradiance forecasting with calibrated uncertainty estimates suited for grid management applications at arid-climate sites.

title: History-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for real-time robot navigation in dynamic industrial environments
abstract: The advent of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has significantly advanced the capabilities of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) in navigating complex and dynamic environments. However, existing DRL models often struggle in industrial settings characterized by their unpredictable and changing nature. To address this challenge, we propose a novel History-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning (HA-DRL) framework designed to enhance AMRs’ navigation capabilities by incorporating historical context into the learning process. The HA-DRL framework enriches the decision-making process by leveraging past experiences, enabling robots to make informed decisions in real-time, thus improving navigation efficiency and safety. Through extensive experimentation in both simulated and real-world industrial settings, we demonstrate that HA-DRL consistently outperforms traditional DRL approaches in terms of navigation performance. This research highlights the importance of historical context in developing more adaptable, efficient, and safe autonomous navigation systems for industrial applications. The experimental video is available at https://youtu.be/6LQtWLcwzTg .

title: Capability Scaling-Down Laws for LLM Compression
abstract: LLM compression reduces inference costs and memory requirements, but selecting a method and configuration remains largely empirical because comparable resource reductions can produce different capability losses. We systematically investigate capability scaling-down laws for LLM compression across pruning, quantization, and distillation. Our framework measures capability loss in mathematics, code generation, and question answering, and relates these measurements to model size, training stage, compression settings, data availability, and training exposure. We develop simple predictive relations and evaluate their accuracy, measurement efficiency, and generalization to unseen configurations and model states. Sharing the density response across pruning levels halves the configuration measurements needed to fit a pruning predictor: on new Pythia states, on pre-registered OLMo-2 test states and under Wanda pruning, the compact relation matches a regression fitted with all measurements on math and code to within 0.020 nats per token, with coefficients refitted for each setting. Controlled distillation experiments show that the cost of heavy data reuse recurs across question-answering distributions, while the net benefit depends on the evaluation distribution. We further evaluate the decision value of these predictions by comparing numerical selection with configuration medians and fixed method priorities. Independent evaluations across two model families show that selection captures most of the available cross-method benefit for question answering within the tested candidate sets, where a fixed method priority attains the same regret, with smaller opportunities for mathematics and code. These results clarify the predictive scope of capability scaling-down laws and their use in compression method selection. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/LabRAI/scaling_down_law.

title: DecomVoxel: Harnessing 3D-Native Priors with Guided In-situ Denoising Optimization for Decompositional Scene Reconstruction
abstract: Decompositional scene reconstruction aims to reconstruct high-quality objects and background, yet existing methods still struggle with the level of quality under heavy occlusions. While generative priors offer a potential solution, 2D image-based priors often suffer from multi-view inconsistency due to a lack of 3D awareness. Conversely, 3D-native priors provide stronger structural inductive biases but frequently lead to spatial drift and misalignment within complex scenes. To address these issues, we propose DecomVoxel, formulating object completion as a guided in-situ denoising optimization that bridges 3D-native priors with neural scene reconstruction. Our framework introduces a reformulated epsilon-based distillation loss to ensure stable latent refinement, alongside adaptive spatial guidance that utilizes occupied and vacant anchors with temporal annealing to suppress generative hallucinations and mitigate spatial drift. Experiments on Replica and ScanNet++ show that DecomVoxel significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods while faithfully preserving the original spatial layout, structural fidelity, and style-consistent texture. Our method pushes the boundary of decompositional reconstruction by delivering high-quality textured meshes with clean topology, geometry, and appearance, providing a robust solution for the decompositional reconstruction of complex real-world scenes. Code is available at https://github.com/DecomVoxel/DecomVoxel.

title: CrossGMN: Graph Metanetworks for Cross-Architecture Weight-Space Transformations
abstract: Weight-space networks operate directly on parameters of other neural networks, enabling tasks such as predicting model properties, editing trained models, and generating weights. Weight-space symmetries such as neuron permutations make equivariance a key design principle. However, existing equivariant weight-space architectures have primarily been studied for transformations that preserve the network architecture. In contrast, many practical transformations, including model compression and upscaling, map a trained source network into a target network with a different architecture. In this setting, the source and target permutation symmetries act on different parameter spaces, making equivariance less straightforward to formulate. Our key idea for addressing this mismatch is to reformulate cross-architecture operators with two inputs: a trained source network and an initialization of the target network. This lets us define equivariant cross-architecture operators that refine the initialization of the target network using information from the source network, while being invariant to source-network permutations and equivariant to target-network permutations. Based on this formulation, we introduce CrossGMN, a graph metanetwork that jointly processes both networks through symmetry-preserving cross-network message passing. We prove CrossGMN is universal for continuous cross-architecture operators on compact sets under a general-position assumption. We evaluate CrossGMN for model compression, predicting a smaller network's parameters to accelerate subsequent knowledge distillation. Across 2-D and 3-D INRs and image classification with MLPs, CNNs, and Vision Transformers, CrossGMN speeds up distillation by up to 8.89x, transfers across datasets without retraining (3.78x), and a single model can accelerate compression from heterogeneous source architectures into a common target architecture.

title: Concept Driven Domain Adaptation: Finding an Abstract Needle in a Haystack
abstract: Science teachers frequently search for documentary excerpts not by describing what appears on screen, but by querying the abstract concepts they intend to teach. This use case exposes a limitation of existing language-based video moment retrieval methods, which typically assume that queries describe observable events, whereas instructional search requires retrieving concrete visual phenomena that instantiate an underlying scientific principle. We study this setting as concept-to-example video retrieval, an abstract-needle-in-a-haystack problem where compact curriculum concepts must be grounded in temporally sparse documentary evidence. To bridge this abstraction gap, we propose Concept-Driven Domain Adaptation (CDDA), a three-stage framework for adapting two-tower vision-language models to concept-level retrieval. CDDA treats concepts as intermediate semantic anchors: it first structures the textual embedding space with textbook and teacher-handbook example-concept pairs, then transfers this concept-aware geometry to documentary visuals under a frozen visual encoder, and finally jointly adapts both encoders with sparse visual concept supervision. From a geometric perspective, this staged alignment reduces text-concept and vision-concept angular gaps, thereby encouraging concept-level adaptation while preserving the pretrained model's concrete image description alignment. On a curated middle-school physics retrieval benchmark, CDDA achieves stronger pedagogically oriented concept retrieval than several competitive multimodal baselines, including Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, while maintaining concrete image-text matching after adaptation.

title: Supervised Classification of Civil Unrest-Related Posts in Twitter/X Data: Evidence from the CUT Dataset
abstract: Social media platforms provide rapid public reports during demonstrations, crises, and civil unrest, but the volume and noise of user-generated content make manual monitoring impractical. This retrospective text-classification study evaluated supervised machine learning models for identifying incident-related civil unrest posts using the Civil Unrest on Twitter (CUT) dataset. The dataset consisted of 4,381 manually annotated English-language Twitter posts collected from 42 countries between 2014 and 2019. The analysis used keyword-based collection, language filtering, crowdsourced annotation, unigram bag-of-words representation, class-balancing procedures reported for the dataset, and supervised classification. Five algorithms were evaluated on the selected balanced dataset: Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosted Decision Trees, and Convolutional Neural Network, each with and without hashtag features. In the original distribution, 690 posts were incident-related and 3,691 were non-incident-related. Dataset 2, containing 6,978 observations with 27% incident-related and 73% non-incident-related posts, was selected because it produced stronger minority-class performance. Incident-related F1-scores ranged from 0.845 to 0.915, and AUC values ranged from 0.958 to 0.977. SVM Model 1, trained with hashtag features, achieved the highest incident-related F1-score (0.915). The findings suggest that supervised classification may provide a useful filtering layer for analyst-supported civil unrest monitoring. However, the framework was evaluated on historical batch data rather than in a prospective streaming setting; therefore, real-time validation, transparent governance, multilingual testing, and stronger ethical safeguards are required before operational deployment.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AND ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION-MAKING IN UNIVERSITY SPORTS MANAGEMENT IN RIVERS STATE, NIGERIA
abstract: This study found that AI adoption significantly predicted administrative decision-making and sports management efficiency among university sports administrators in Rivers State, Nigeria. The study adopted a cross-sectional correlational research design. The study involved sports administrators from the University of Port Harcourt, Rivers State University, Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, and Federal University of Environment and Technology. The estimated population was 160 sports administrators, from which a sample of 114 respondents was selected using the Taro Yamane formula. Eighty-nine completed questionnaires were retrieved, representing a 78% return rate. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measuring AI adoption, administrative decision-making, and sports management efficiency. Descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation, were used to answer the research questions, while simple linear regression was employed to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 significance level. The findings showed that AI adoption had a strong perceived influence on administrative decision-making (grand mean = 3.03). Regression analysis further indicated that AI adoption significantly predicted administrative decision-making, R = .614, R² = .377, β = .614, F(1, 87) = 52.61, p < .001. AI adoption also demonstrated a strong perceived influence on sports management efficiency (grand mean = 3.06) and significantly predicted management efficiency, R = .638, R² = .407, β = .638, F(1, 87) = 59.72, p < .001. The study concludes that AI adoption represents a promising mechanism for improving decision quality and operational efficiency in university sports management. The study recommended, among other things, that university sports management adopt AI-supported administrative systems for planning, scheduling, information management, resource allocation, and monitoring of sporting programs.

title: A Pre-Registered Evaluation Framework for Architecture-Induced Cognitive Performance in Large Language Models
abstract: This protocol pre-registers a controlled benchmark designed to test whether the ALEX cognitive architecture produces measurable changes in analytical performance when applied to the same underlying large language model used in a baseline condition. ALEX is treated as an orchestration and governance architecture rather than as a separate foundation model. The benchmark therefore isolates architecture as the principal experimental variable. The study uses 120 tasks across 12 cognitive categories, paired baseline/ALEX responses, blinded and randomized A/B evaluation, a pre-specified 100-point ALEX Cognitive Quality Score (ACQS), explicit error penalties, category-level diagnostics, and pre-specified rules for statistical analysis, success, partial success, and failure. The protocol is deliberately symmetric: it rewards thesis falsification, uncertainty calibration, expectation-gap reasoning, regime awareness and disciplined assertion, but also penalizes excessive caution, unnecessary complexity, verbosity, generic risk enumeration, and failure to answer a well-posed question. The benchmark is intended to determine not merely whether ALEX produces different answers, but where, if anywhere, its architecture creates reproducible cognitive advantages or costs.

title: Constrained Decoding for Structural Error Suppression in Dependency Tree Generation with Large Language Models
abstract: Abstract— In the field of syntactic parsing, fine-tuning large language models to generate a sentence’s syntactic structure in bracket form is a promising approach. Existing fine-tuned models demonstrate high values of syntax parsing metrics; however, in some cases they generate an incorrect bracket sequence (for example, with an unbalanced number of opening and closing parentheses). Therefore, this study aims to develop a method to reduce the number of incorrectly generated sequences. A system of constraints has been introduced on the set of tokens generated at each stage of the large language model. The implemented method was tested on four fine-tuned models (adapted and non-adapted with 4 and 8 billion parameters) on the SynTagRus dependency tree dataset. For all models, the number of incorrectly generated sequences decreased. However, some sentences were not parsed, because the LLMs generated an excessively long token sequence and were interrupted. The code for this study is publicly available.

title: Teleseismic case identification results of the DiTing 0.1b phase-picking model
abstract: Phase-picking models are usually trained on regional waveforms, and their performance on teleseismic records requires further examination using real data. This study takes the DiTing 0.1b phase-picking model of the DiTing seismic large-model series as the study object and carries out a case-based test of teleseismic phase identification within the DTFlowPro framework, using 15 global earthquakes of M5.0～5.9 that occurred from 22 to 31 December 2024. Two detection branches, the native-sampling branch and a 20 Hz resampling branch, were built. The candidates were fused by taking the union of time-clustered picks. The two branches showed clear complementarity. For P phases, 286 stations produced detections in both branches, 179 only in the native-sampling branch, and 40 only in the 20 Hz branch. The corresponding numbers for the S phase were 29, 19, and 25. The fused detections exactly matched the union of the two branches, and the station detection rates increased to 12.03% for the P phase and 1.74% for the S phase, 0.94 and 0.45 percentage points higher than those of the best single branch. The fused P detection rate decreased from 74.19% at 0°～10° to 4.19% at 90°～100°, and the fused S detection rate decreased from 58.06% at 0°～10° to below 8% beyond 10°. Among the combinations of three association methods and three fixed-depth location objective functions, the combination of native sampling, robust residual iteration, and the weighted L2 norm produced the smallest median epicentral error of 23.66 km. The event-building program dtevent of DTFlowPro merged 1102 phase picks and 359 origin solutions into 15 earthquakes, with no missing, incorrectly merged, or incorrectly split catalog events. This case-based evaluation of 15 typical teleseismic earthquakes indicates that, under catalog-guided conditions, the DiTing 0.1b model provides usable identification of teleseismic P phases within 90°, while the identification of S phases and of P phases beyond 90° remains limited. Because these conclusions are based on a limited number of cases, they should not be extrapolated to an assessment of teleseismic monitoring capability.

title: Towards Hijacking Interactions in Virtual Reality
abstract: We identify and study a new Virtual Reality Interaction Manipulation (VRIM) attack, where a remote attacker takes control of a user's interaction with the VR system, by trapping the user inside a malicious app that masquerades as the full VR interface. Once trapped, the user's interactions with apps, services, and other users can be recorded and modified without their knowledge. We build a prototype of VRIM on Meta Quest headsets and conduct an IRB-approved user study to validate its feasibility and efficacy. We disclosed VRIM and potential defenses to Meta, who responded positively. Our work emphasizes the need for new security measures tailored to the unique immersive nature of VR systems.

title: When and how anthropomorphic AI avatars relate to user engagement intentions: roles of emotional connection, perceived authenticity and technological familiarity
abstract: Purpose This study examines when and how anthropomorphic AI service avatars shape user engagement intentions in digital commerce. Drawing primarily on computers are social actors (CASA) theory and using parasocial interaction (PSI) as a bounded interpretive lens, it examines emotional connection as an encounter-specific affective mechanism and perceived authenticity and technological familiarity as theoretically focal contingencies operating at different stages of the engagement process. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 employed a between-subjects experiment that manipulated higher versus lower levels of bundled visual-form anthropomorphism. Study 2 used a three-wave survey of online shoppers to re-examine the focal relationships in prior AI-avatar service encounters. Mediation, moderation, and conditional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Findings Study 1 shows that higher visual-form anthropomorphism increases user engagement intention, with emotional connection accounting for a meaningful but partial share of the effect. Study 2 provides associative support for the core relationships, although the association between anthropomorphism and emotional connection is comparatively modest. Perceived authenticity strengthens the theoretically focal association between anthropomorphism and emotional connection, while technological familiarity strengthens the association between emotional connection and engagement intention. The findings indicate that emotional connection represents one mechanism among multiple affective, cognitive and evaluative pathways linking anthropomorphic AI avatars with engagement intentions. Originality/value This study advances interactive marketing research by identifying emotional connection as a meaningful but partial encounter-level mechanism linking AI-avatar anthropomorphism with engagement intentions. It further demonstrates that perceived authenticity and technological familiarity condition the theoretically focal stages of this process, while the dominant direct component highlights the need for a multiple-pathway, rather than exclusively affective, account of AI-avatar engagement.

title: Spontaneity and authorship: a Kantian account of human authorship in copyright law
abstract: Generative AI has revived a neglected question in copyright law: why must authors be human? Courts and copyright offices have largely answered through statutory interpretation, but the underlying jurisprudence remains underdeveloped. This article draws on Kant’s theory of publication and spontaneity to argue that copyright protects an imputable communicative act. A copyright work transcends its status as a produced object to exist fundamentally as a public address attributable to a rational subject capable of authorising its communication. The article grounds this account in the architecture of Kant’s Doctrine of Right: the mandate that authorises publication is a relation between persons, modelled on the Roman mandatum, and the standing from which it issues is an exercise of the author’s innate right of communicative freedom. Current AI systems possess the capacity to generate outputs, yet they remain incapable of originating communicative acts or issuing mandates in the Kantian sense. The article further develops a Mandate Test for human-AI collaboration and concludes that the human authorship requirement follows from the nature of authorship itself, not merely from historical practice or legislative convention.

title: Ultra-short-term PV power prediction based on a dual-stream CNN-GRU-attention framework
abstract: Aiming at the challenges of data noise and cumulative error in photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting, this paper proposes a dat a and model dual-closed-loop ultra-short-term forecasting framework. At the data end, the interquartile range (IQR) method and forward-backward interpolation are utilized to reconstruct outliers, while the Spearman coefficient and sine-cosine encoding are combined to optimize meteorological and temporal features. At the model end, a dual-stream network is constructed using a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) strategy. The historical stream extracts multi-scale temporal features using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) - Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) - Attention mechanism, whereas the future stream resolves weather trends using a GRU. Simulation results show that the model's coefficient of determination reaches 0.983, and simulation comparisons with other models and ablation studies have demonstrated the superiority of the proposed model and the effectiveness of its core components.

title: A Composable AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for 3D-IC Thermal Modeling
abstract: Accurate thermal analysis of heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC packages is essential yet computationally prohibitive. A single full-package FEM simulation can take hours, while AI-based surrogates treat the entire stack as a monolithic prediction target and must be retrained whenever the die count or topology changes. To address this limitation, this work proposes Domain-Decomposed AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for Thermal Analysis (DAIST), a composable thermal solver that decomposes the global package simulation into block-level subdomain problems, replaces subdomain solvers with neural operators, and couples them through iterative exchanges of interfacial temperature and heat flux. This local-to-global architecture eliminates the topology lock-in of monolithic models: block-level neural operators can be directly reused in unseen package assemblies without retraining. The iterative coupling strategy further provides a controllable accuracy-runtime tradeoff, where the iteration budget can be adjusted to trade accuracy for runtime. Evaluated on a multi-chiplet system and an advanced packaging system, DAIST achieves up to $178\times$ speedup over traditional FEM solvers with mean temperature errors of 0.068% and 0.323%, respectively, while demonstrating cross-topology reuse of block-level models across structurally distinct package assemblies.

title: Watch, Infer, Coordinate: Inferring Robot Partner Constraints for Zero-Shot Coordination
abstract: Robots operating in the physical world will increasingly need to coordinate with other robots, particularly in manipulation tasks where an object may be too large or heavy for a single robot to carry alone. Physical limitations caused by hardware degradation or actuator faults can restrict the actions a robot can reliably execute, yet these limitations may be unknown to its partner. We study whether a helper can infer a robot partner's physical constraints from observing it coordinate with another robot, then use the inferred capability to coordinate with the same partner on a new task. This is difficult because a demonstration shows what the constrained robot did, but not what it could have done. In physically coupled tasks, the other robot may also compensate for its limitations, making those limitations difficult to identify from the constrained robot's behavior alone. Our key insight is that these constraints shape the joint behavior of the team, making the actions of both robots informative about the constrained partner's capability. We introduce Watch, Infer, Coordinate, a benchmark spanning three physically coupled manipulation settings, together with an inference approach that scores candidate constraints using observed joint behavior. Across all three settings, our method substantially improves constraint inference and zero-shot coordination, approaching an oracle with access to the true constraints.

title: Invertibility of structured perturbations of singular matrices over unital rings
abstract: In this article, we study the invertibility of matrices of the form A+EDF, where A and D are square matrices over a unital, not necessarily commutative, ring and A is singular. Under natural hypotheses on kernels and images, we prove that A+EDF is invertible if and only if D is invertible, and obtain an explicit formula for the inverse of A+EDF by purely algebraic methods. When the coefficient ring is stably finite, or more specifically a field, we obtain an invertibility criterion under weaker hypotheses. Our results extend and sharpen a theorem of Eriksson and Nordqvist for complex matrices.

title: Towards a Cloud Fog Edge System for Smart Building
abstract: In this article, we present our vision and recent advancements toward creating a decentralized system capable of learning from real-time data within buildings to support sustainable and privacy-preserving smart environments. Our approach promotes the concept of the building itself as the data center, aligning with the principles of edge computing to safeguard confidentiality and reduce reliance on external cloud infrastructure. This is particularly valuable in humanitarian contexts, where data sovereignty, energy efficiency, and infrastructure constraints are critical. We detail a lightweight, "Kubernetes-like" orchestration framework for deploying AI services within such environments and demonstrate our progress in implementing AI algorithms on low-power, cost-effective microcontrollers such as those in the Arduino ecosystem. By enabling in-situ learning directly on sensors or microcontrollers, our work aims to bring intelligent services to resource-limited settings, fostering autonomy, resilience, and sustainable development in vulnerable or underserved communities. The contributions in this article are related, firstly, to our project "Online Machine Learning Algorithms for Embedded Systems" and the evaluation of two new online algorithms. Secondly, we envision a cloud-fog-edge architecture based on the KOptim and FIWARE components, and we propose a methodology for coupling them. Experimental results of the online algorithms are also presented, showcasing real-world traces.

We detail a lightweight, "Kubernetes-like" orchestration framework for deploying AI services within such environments and demonstrate our progress in implementing AI algorithms on low-power, cost-effective microcontrollers such as those in the Arduino ecosystem. By enabling in-situ learning directly on sensors or microcontrollers, our work aims to bring intelligent services to resource-limited settings, fostering autonomy, resilience, and sustainable development in vulnerable or underserved communities. The contributions in this article are related, firstly, to our project "Online Machine Learning Algorithms for Embedded Systems" and the evaluation of two new online algorithms. Secondly, we envision a cloud-fog-edge architecture based on the KOptim and FIWARE components, and we propose a methodology for coupling them. Experimental results of the online algorithms are also presented, showcasing real-world traces.

title: Localisation-Aware Uncertainty for Pretrained Object Detection
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for deploying object detectors when distribution/covariate shift and adversarial attacks may occur. Existing approaches often require detector retraining, architectural modification, or repeated inference, which may be infeasible or incur significant overheads. We introduce a lightweight post-hoc evidential meta-model that learns when object localisations should be considered uncertain while keeping the base detector frozen. Our approach automatically identifies localisation-relevant features and uses saliency-guided modification to construct an increasingly challenging curriculum. Detection-level targets combine localisation error, modification level, and prediction instability to guide an evidential meta-model to estimate uncertainty for each predicted bounding box. Our approach requires no changes to the detector and preserves its original localisation outputs. Across adversarial attacks and evaluated strengths, GRACE improves TP-FP AUROC by 22% relative to the strongest comparator in some cases while maintaining in-distribution detection performance.

title: A Quantum Phase Neural Network with Multi-Inputs/Single-Output
abstract: A 35 input/single output quantum phase neural network (QPNN) is proposed to recognize the English letters' A 'and' B 'composed 7*5 of pixels. Each node of the proposed QPNN has the input with 0 or 1. Through normalization and quantum phase encoding, each set of 35 with 0 or 1 digital inputs is encoded into a quantum superposition state described by 35 quantum phases. Then, a quantum rotation gate is used to introduce adjustable phase, and a controlled NOT gate is used to entangle the relative phase between the two inputs. The relationship between the input and output of the network is derived. This paper also derived the phase weight learning training algorithm with adaptive learning rate. The solutions with the recognition probability of 1 is designed, and the analytical expressions for all adjustable phase solutions with zero errors are not unique. The experimental performance is verified on the Qiskit platform. This paper uses phase drive to convert the probability calculation into an analytical polynomial function with adjustable rotation angles in the network, avoiding the bottleneck of generating all 2^35 complex exponential amplitudes and providing an effective way to solve the "exponential wall" problem, which provides a new implementation solution for the practical application of multi-input recognition problems.

title: Lifting the maximally-entangledness assumption in robust self-testing for synchronous games
abstract: Robust self-testing in non-local games allows a classical referee to certify that two untrustworthy players are able to perform a specific quantum strategy up to high precision. Proving robust self-testing results becomes significantly easier when one restricts the allowed strategies to symmetric projective maximally entangled (PME) strategies, which allow natural descriptions in terms of tracial von Neumann algebras. This has been exploited in the celebrated M I P ∗ = R E paper and related articles to prove robust self-testing results for synchronous games when restricting to PME strategies. However, the PME assumptions are not physical, so these results need to be upgraded to make them physically relevant. In this work, we do just that: we prove that any perfect synchronous game which is a robust self-test when restricted to PME strategies, is in fact a robust self-test for all strategies. We then apply our result to the Quantum Low Degree Test to find an efficient n -qubit test.

title: Construction of a Teaching Quality Monitoring and Evaluation System Based on Data Mining Analysis
abstract: In our country, the teacher team construction and management level are constantly improving. It is crucial to enhance education quality, particularly classroom teaching quality. This study explores the application of data mining techniques in teaching quality evaluation. Using a dataset comprising evaluation scores from 10 teachers at a university, we construct a prototype system to demonstrate the proposed methodology, this paper studied the large data mining technology and clustering analysis algorithm, and based on this algorithm, put forward the teaching quality control and evaluation system, and choose a college teacher to students train the system, finally, the application of this system, the application effect is good. The specific conclusions are as follows: (1) compared with Apriori algorithm, FP-growth algorithm and HBE-Apriori algorithm, this algorithm has obvious advantages in operation speed. (2) The theoretical basis of K-mean clustering and the method of evaluating K-mean clustering are given, specific procedures and implementation procedures are given, and finally an example is given to illustrate its process and operation process. There are many ways of evaluation, with an emphasis on analyzing the values of purity and F1. (3) expounds three levels of the platform: performance level, service level and data level. Then, the specific implementation schemes of system initialization design, data collection, data preprocessing and data mining are expounded. (4) There is a close connection between teachers ’education quality and students’ education quality. The corresponding “satisfaction” of “excellent” teachers is 0.8; the education quality of teachers is “good”; if the teaching content is good and the level evaluation confidence is 0.7, the confidence level is 0.5 regardless of whether the level evaluation is satisfactory or basically satisfied, significantly lower than both “good” and “level evaluation”. Another important element is the reasonable arrangement and optimization of the course content. This study employed evaluation scores from ten faculty members at a university as a preliminary pilot dataset to demonstrate the proposed methodological workflow, thereby constructing a prototype system. We explicitly acknowledge that this sample size constitutes the primary limitation of the study, and the generalizability of the conclusions requires further validation. When teaching content is rated as ’excellent,’ the confidence level for a ’satisfactory’ evaluation grade is 0.7; when teaching content is rated as ’good,’ the confidence level for both ’satisfactory’ and ’basically satisfied’ evaluations is 0.5—significantly lower than the level for ’excellent’ teaching content.
